How ready your body is to train today, from 0 to 100. It weighs what the watch measured overnight and your recent training, each against your own normal rather than population averages, and suggests whether the day suits hard training (ready to train, from 70), moderate training (train with care, from 50) or an easy day (take it easy, below 50).

# What goes in
- HRV, 35 %: its recent average against your normal range from the 60 days before the last week, so that the nights being judged are not part of what they are judged against. The average covers the last seven nights with the latest counting most (last night seven times, the night before six times, down to once a week back), so good nights after a poor spell show as recovery within days.
- Sleep, 25 %: last night's sleep score and the average of the last three nights.
- Resting heart rate, 20 %: last night against the nights before.
- Training, 20 %: form against a band that grows with your fitness.

Each part moves the score by its weight, so a low HRV pulls it down as far as its share allows and no further. A part without data leaves its weight to the others.

# Illness
A breathing rate clearly above usual, together with low HRV or a raised resting heart rate, holds readiness at 40 or below. Breathing rate has no weight of its own, and this combination is a common early sign of an illness, when training is best left alone.

# How much to trust it
The HRV comparison has the strongest research behind it: in HRV-guided training studies, easy days whenever the week's HRV fell below its normal range gave results at least as good as a fixed plan (Vesterinen 2016; Javaloyes 2019). The weights are PacingLab's own choice, not a validated score. A first score appears after two weeks of nights with HRV, a week for the recent average and a week for a first baseline, and is marked provisional; once the baseline has 14 nights, about three weeks in, it is settled, and it keeps improving over four to eight weeks.

# The week
The small chart shows the score of each of the last seven days, computed from the data up to that day, on the bands of the three levels.

Your own answer, once in the morning, from 1 (exhausted) to 5 (fully rested).

How rested you feel is the one part of sleep health a watch cannot measure. In training research, simple daily ratings like this one follow training load at least as well as most measurements (Saw 2016).

PacingLab keeps your answers with the night they follow. Once you answer, the question leaves Today; Sleep > Night shows the answer and lets you change it, for any morning, at the bottom under How you felt and the score. Once a few weeks have collected, that card shows how well the sleep score matches how you feel.
How hard was the gym session?

One tap for how hard the whole session felt, from 1 (very, very easy) to 10 (maximal).\n\nHeart rate reacts little to lifting, so the rating is what gives a gym session its training load: the rating times the minutes, known as session RPE (Foster 2001). Only gym sessions ask, and only until the day after. The rating can be changed on the session\'s page.

Load, VO2max and HRV in one word
Not enough training yet: the status needs four weeks of load.

Where your training stands over the last weeks, in one word. Productive training builds fitness and maintaining holds it; peaking and recovery are lighter spells in which the body absorbs the work before; detraining loses fitness; overreaching, unproductive and strained warn that the body is not keeping up. Readiness is about today; this is about the trend.\n\nIt comes from three things: your recent load against your usual (fatigue over fitness), how VO2max moved over four weeks, and HRV\'s recent average against its normal range. Tap for Training > Load, where the reasons are listed.

Forecast by Open-Meteo (open-meteo.com, CC BY 4.0), which blends the national weather services' models; in Denmark that includes DMI's.

Only your approximate position, rounded to about 1 km, is sent, with no other data. A forecast is reused for 20 minutes while you stay nearby.

Feels like combines temperature, wind and humidity. Dew point is the measure of humidity that matters when running in heat: the higher it is, the less your sweat evaporates and cools you. Wind is in metres per second. Each hour shows its chance of rain from 20 % up.
The forecast needs your approximate location. Only a position rounded to about 1 km is sent to Open-Meteo.
